transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Yeah, thanks for fitting me in. Honestly, I’ve been putting this off for a really long time, probably years if I’m being completely honest with myself, but things have just gotten to a point where I can't ignore it anymore. I work in video production—I'm an editor and sometimes a camera operator, mostly for corporate clients and some documentary stuff—and it's a fast-paced environment, which I usually love, but lately... well, what finally scared me into coming in is that I keep making these incredibly dumb technical mistakes. And the thing is, I know better. I've been doing this for over a decade since I got my bachelor's, so it's not like I don't know the workflow. But I'll do things like label the camera cards wrong after a shoot, which is a nightmare for the assistant editors, or I'll completely miss a timecode note from a director. Just last week, I exported a final client cut—a cut that was going straight to the client for final approval—and it had the wrong lower-third graphic on the CEO's interview. And the craziest part is, I swore I checked it. I sat there, I watched the timeline, I thought I checked it, but I still sent it out wrong. It's just so embarrassing and it's starting to really affect my reputation with the producers, and I just... I don't know why I can't seem to catch these things anymore.
When you make these mistakes, how do you feel emotionally? Are you feeling more anxious, down, or maybe both?

Gosh, I don't... I mean, I guess I wouldn't use either of those words exactly? It's not like I'm sitting around feeling depressed or crying about it, and I wouldn't say I'm having panic attacks or anything. It's more like... well, when I get that email from a producer, like with that CEO video I mentioned, the second I see the subject line or the timecode notes, my stomach just completely drops. But it's this very immediate, intense frustration. I get so incredibly mad at myself. 

When I realized the lower-third was wrong, I literally jumped up from my desk and just started pacing around the edit bay, rubbing my face, just thinking, "How did I do this again? How did I miss this?" I couldn't even sit still to fix it right away because I was just so agitated with my own brain. So I don't know if that's anxiety? My mom is a very anxious person—she worries about absolutely everything, like if the weather is going to be bad or if she left the stove on—and I'm really not like that at all. I'm usually a pretty upbeat person, actually. I like being on the go, I like juggling a million things on set, I'm always moving. 

So it's not a lingering sadness or a constant worry. It's just... in the moment, my heart pounds, I want to pull my hair out, I fix the mistake as fast as humanly possible, and then I just feel incredibly annoyed and embarrassed. Like I'm a fraud who somehow tricked people into hiring me, even though I have the degree and the experience. But then I'm on to the next project and I'm fine again, until the next stupid mistake happens. Does that make sense? I just haven't really thought of it as being down or anxious, just... infuriating.

Outside of your work environment, do you find it hard to stay focused or concentrate on tasks, like following through with plans, staying organized, or remembering important details in your day-to-day life?

Honestly, I haven't really noticed anything like that? Or maybe I just don't put myself in situations where I have to sit still and concentrate when I'm off the clock. Because when I'm not working, I'm pretty much always on the go. I don't really make rigid plans that I have to follow through on in the first place, so there's nothing to really fall behind on, if that makes sense. I'm more of a fly-by-the-seat-of-my-pants kind of person. 

My weekends are usually just packed with doing whatever catches my eye. Like, just this past Saturday, I woke up and decided I was going to finally clean out my hall closet, so I pulled absolutely everything out into the hallway. But then my friend texted me about this outdoor vintage flea market happening downtown, and I love vintage camera gear, so I just left the boxes in the hall and went to the market. And then from there we ended up biking around the lake, and then I grabbed dinner with another group of friends, and I didn't actually put the closet back together until Sunday night. But I wouldn't say I lost focus on the closet, I just... shifted gears? I like being busy. I like bouncing from one thing to the next. 

As for staying organized, I mean, my apartment is a little cluttered, sure, I've got cables and hard drives and stuff around, but I know where everything is. And remembering details... I pay my bills. I don't really forget major life things. It's really just the work stuff that's the problem. Because at work, I *have* to sit in front of the monitors in a dark edit bay for eight or ten hours, and I can't just get up and go bike around a lake when I feel restless. 

At home, if I feel jittery or like I need to move, I just go do something. I'll go for a run, or I'll suddenly decide to rearrange my living room furniture at 10 PM. Even when I try to just relax and watch a movie, I'm usually also scrolling on my phone or folding laundry or stretching, because I just can't stand doing only one thing at a time. It feels physically uncomfortable to just sit and exist, you know? Like my legs literally start aching to move. But I wouldn't call that a problem with focus or forgetting things, really. It's just how I've always been. I just like to keep moving.
Have you ever been told by someone close to you—like a friend, family member, or partner—that you have trouble sitting still, act impulsively, or seem distracted even in non-work situations?

Oh, definitely. I mean, my friends definitely notice that I can't sit still—like my ex used to absolutely hate sitting next to me at the movie theater because I'd constantly be shifting around or shaking the row, and he'd always put his hand on my leg to physically hold it down, which honestly just made me feel trapped and want to move even more. 

But honestly, where it gets pointed out the absolute most—and it's actually kind of embarrassing now that I'm saying it out loud—is by my coworkers. Especially when we have to sit in the bay with the directors or producers and watch a full twenty-minute cut down. It's usually super quiet in there, just the audio from the monitors, and I just... I physically cannot just sit there like a statue. In edit reviews I’m constantly clicking a pen—usually one of those retractable Pilot ones because I just desperately need something to do with my hands—or I'm bouncing my knee under the table, or rolling my chair back and forth. We have these really nice ergonomic chairs on a hard floor, and I'll just sort of drift back and forth or swivel while I'm watching the screen. 

I don't even realize I'm doing it half the time! I'll just be totally zoned in on the video, and then suddenly a producer will turn around and give me this look, or ask me to please stop clicking because it's distracting them. It's gotten to the point where people have started joking that they can hear me before they see me. Like, the assistant editors will hear the squeak of my shoes or the tap-tap-tap of my foot down the hall and they're like, "Oh, here she comes, brace yourselves." 

So, yeah, people definitely comment on it. Constantly, actually. I just always brushed it off as having a lot of kinetic energy, you know? Like I said, I'm a fast-paced person. I never really thought about it as being "distracted" or anything bad, just... a quirk? Just my body needing to do something while my brain is working. But they definitely notice the moving around.
Looking back, were you noticeably more active, impulsive, or had trouble focusing when you were a child—like in school or at home—compared to other kids your age?

Oh wow, yeah. I mean, if you asked my parents, they would probably laugh and then talk your ear off for an hour about what a handful I was. It goes way, way back. Like, even in elementary school, my teachers were constantly having to move my desk. I remember it happening pretty much every single year. 

In third grade, I had Mrs. Gallagher, and she had this whole strict seating chart system, but I never stayed in my assigned spot. I was just always out of my seat. I’d get up to sharpen my pencil for the fifth time, or go look out the window, or I'd just wander over to the reading corner because I felt like it. And the blurting out answers—oh my gosh, it was constant. The teacher would ask a question about, I don't know, state capitals or a math problem, and I would just yell the answer out before she even finished the sentence, let alone called on anyone with their hand raised. I just couldn't hold it in! It was like the thought had to exit my mouth the exact second it formed in my brain. 

And I was always bothering my classmates, too. I'd be tapping on their desks, or whispering to them during silent reading, or leaning way over into their space to see what they were drawing. And the crazy thing is, I honestly wouldn't even realize I was doing it until the teacher snapped my name. I’d be completely oblivious that I was being disruptive. 

So they'd move my desk. First they'd move it to the front row, right by the teacher's desk, thinking that would keep me in line. But then I'd just talk to the teacher. Then they'd move me to the back corner, so I wouldn't distract the kids behind me. I think in fourth grade they even put my desk totally separate from the little group pods everyone else got to sit in, which I absolutely hated because then I just wanted to turn around constantly to see what everyone else was doing. My mom was always getting notes sent home or getting pulled aside at parent-teacher conferences. They'd always say the same thing—that I was a bright kid, but I was "disruptive" or needed to learn how to stay in my chair. 

And at home, it was exactly the same. I was the kid climbing the doorframes in the hallway, jumping off the back of the sofa, just a total tornado. My poor older brother couldn't ever just play a quiet game of Monopoly with me because I’d get too antsy waiting for my turn and I'd either accidentally knock the board over by fidgeting, or I'd just wander off into the kitchen completely and forget we were playing. So, yeah, I guess compared to other kids who could just sit cross-legged on the rug during storytime and actually stay there, I was noticeably... a lot more active. It’s always been like this, really. I just never stopped moving.

Can you think of any situations outside of work—like in personal relationships, school responsibilities, or managing daily tasks—where your difficulty staying still, trouble focusing, or acting without thinking has caused problems or negative consequences?

Honestly, outside of work... I mean, I guess it depends on what you call a "problem." Like, sure, my friends get a little annoyed if I interrupt them during a story because a thought just popped into my head and I absolutely have to say it right that second before it vanishes. Or, you know, my mom will sigh when I visit and I immediately start reorganizing her kitchen counters instead of just sitting on the couch to chat with her. But they know me, you know? They know I’m just... energetic. It doesn't ruin my relationships. And managing my daily tasks, well, I might leave a closet totally destroyed for a weekend like I said, but I get it done eventually. So it doesn't really cause any *major* negative consequences in my personal life. 

But where it *is* actually causing a massive problem—and I know you asked about outside of work, but this is what's really keeping me up at night and honestly the whole reason I realized I needed to talk to someone—is on set. It’s getting really, really bad. 

I’ve been a camera operator for a while now, and my actual camera work is really good. Like, my framing, my lighting, my eye for a shot—everyone agrees it's top-notch. But because I can't just stand perfectly still behind the tripod, or because I'm always fidgeting with the rig, or bouncing my leg when we're waiting for the talent to get out of hair and makeup... people misinterpret it. 

My producers have started trusting me less on complex shoots. You know, the really big, high-stakes ones where there are a million moving parts and everyone needs to be totally locked in and quiet? They see me pacing around or tapping my foot or adjusting things that don't need adjusting, and they think I'm not paying attention or that I'm a liability, even though I am completely focused on the shot! 

And the absolute worst part is, my chance at moving into a senior director of photography role has been slipping despite the quality of my camera work. I have the reel for it, my portfolio is exactly what they want, I've put in the years... but they’ve been handing the lead spots to people who honestly have half my eye for composition, just because those guys can stand perfectly still like statues for three hours without making a peep. It’s just incredibly frustrating. It feels so unfair that my actual technical skills are being completely overshadowed just because my body refuses to stay still. So, yeah, the consequences are definitely there, it's just hitting me the hardest in my career.

Can you think of any situations outside of work—like in personal relationships, school responsibilities, or managing daily tasks—where your difficulty staying still, trouble focusing, or acting without thinking has caused problems or negative consequences?

Well, like I kind of just started getting into a second ago, outside of work it really isn't the end of the world. I mean, my friends and family just kind of accept that I'm a human pinball. They know I'm going to interrupt them or pace around the living room, and it doesn't really ruin those relationships. But the real negative consequences—the stuff that actually has me sitting here talking to you today—is what's happening on set. I know you're asking about my personal life, but I just can't stress enough how much this is destroying me professionally. 

My producers have literally started trusting me less on complex shoots. It's so obvious, too. If we're doing a really intricate, high-stakes setup and I'm shifting my weight around or tapping my fingers on the rig while we wait for the lighting cues, I can actually see them looking at me out of the corner of their eyes like I'm not paying attention. Which is just crazy, because I am completely locked in on the shot! But they just see the physical movement and immediately think I'm some kind of liability. 

And the most devastating part of all of this, the thing that just makes me want to pull my hair out, is that my chance at moving into a senior director of photography role has been completely slipping. It's just slipping right through my fingers, and it's happening despite the quality of my camera work. I mean, my reels are fantastic, my composition is spot-on, everyone knows I have a great eye, but because I can't just stand there frozen like a statue for three hours straight, they're passing me over. They're giving the lead spots to people who honestly don't even have half the technical skill or vision that I do, just because those guys can stand perfectly still. It's just so incredibly frustrating to know my work is top-tier, but this... this inability to just stay put is what's actually tanking my career. So, yeah, the consequences are definitely there, they're just hitting my livelihood.

patient.answer:
Honestly, outside of work... I mean, I guess it depends on what you call a "problem." Like, sure, my friends get a little annoyed if I interrupt them during a story because a thought just popped into my head and I absolutely have to say it right that second before it vanishes. Or, you know, my mom will sigh when I visit and I immediately start reorganizing her kitchen counters instead of just sitting on the couch to chat with her. But they know me, you know? They know I’m just... energetic. It doesn't ruin my relationships. And managing my daily tasks, well, I might leave a closet totally destroyed for a weekend like I said, but I get it done eventually. So it doesn't really cause any *major* negative consequences in my personal life. 

But where it *is* actually causing a massive problem—and I know you asked about outside of work, but this is what's really keeping me up at night and honestly the whole reason I realized I needed to talk to someone—is on set. It’s getting really, really bad. 

I’ve been a camera operator for a while now, and my actual camera work is really good. Like, my framing, my lighting, my eye for a shot—everyone agrees it's top-notch. But because I can't just stand perfectly still behind the tripod, or because I'm always fidgeting with the rig, or bouncing my leg when we're waiting for the talent to get out of hair and makeup... people misinterpret it. 

My producers have started trusting me less on complex shoots. You know, the really big, high-stakes ones where there are a million moving parts and everyone needs to be totally locked in and quiet? They see me pacing around or tapping my foot or adjusting things that don't need adjusting, and they think I'm not paying attention or that I'm a liability, even though I am completely focused on the shot! 

And the absolute worst part is, my chance at moving into a senior director of photography role has been slipping despite the quality of my camera work. I have the reel for it, my portfolio is exactly what they want, I've put in the years... but they’ve been handing the lead spots to people who honestly have half my eye for composition, just because those guys can stand perfectly still like statues for three hours without making a peep. It’s just incredibly frustrating. It feels so unfair that my actual technical skills are being completely overshadowed just because my body refuses to stay still. So, yeah, the consequences are definitely there, it's just hitting me the hardest in my career.
